name: Time to focus on Kenya's labour force

content.title: Time to focus on Kenya's labour force
content.summary: Exploring the role of different actors in safeguarding the welfare of labour in Kenya.

media.caption: Employees working in a butchery
media.alt: Time to focus on Kenya's labour force

content.text: Employees are a critical factor in the production process and a key catalyst to the growth of national economies and private enterprise. To safeguard their welfare, it is critical to consider factors such as a safe working environment, humane working conditions, access to health care and practical wages.

The importance of addressing workers' concerns and needs cannot be overemphasized, as they are entitled to a set of rights as guaranteed in their respective countries' labour laws and international conventions. In Kenya, the government and labour unions have attempted to address concerns regarding labour laws and the treatment of workers over the decades, yet a lot of work still needs to be done.

Labour Day, also known as International Workers' Day, is celebrated in Kenya on the 1st of May. Over the years, the Central Organization of Trade Union (COTU), together with the Ministry of Labour, have taken the lead in commemorating this day with the sole obligation of ensuring workers' needs are met by both the government and the Federation of Kenya Employers (FKE). During these celebrations, Kenyan workers, especially those in the lower ranks, make their way to the celebration venues or remain glued to their radio or television eagerly awaiting the official address concerning an increment on the minimum wage and other improvements.

The 2019 Labour Day celebration elicited mixed reactions. The Ministry discussed affordable housing for workers as proposed in President Uhuru Kenyatta's "Big 4 Agenda." This would be implemented by enacting a housing levy of 1.5 per cent of workers' salaries. On the other hand, COTU advocated for a 15 per cent wage increment; however, these propositions were opposed by FKE who raised concerns regarding the sustainability of the high wage bill and rising cost of doing business.
The Aga Khan University's East Africa Institute (EAI) administered a

in 2019 that showed 74 per cent of entry-level staff in the formal sector earn less than 50,000 Kenyan Shillings (about $500 USD) a month. In contrast, 81 per cent of informal sector workers earn less than 25,000 Kenyan Shillings (about $250 USD) a month. Surprisingly, more than half of the entry-level staff had post-secondary education and technical training. According to government regulations, the minimal monthly wage is a mere 13,572 Kenyan Shillings (about $135 USD).

With the rising rate of inflation, this compensation can hardly meet the high cost of living in Kenya. Therefore, this raises major concerns on the return of investment for Kenya's skilled workforce considering the high cost of tertiary education. Most workers in both the formal and informal sectors are not able to finance their basic needs from their meagre wages, resulting in low morale, mental health issues, corruption, and outright crime in an effort to cope with financial hardship.

The government, trade unions and employer associations play a significant role in fighting for livable wages and ensuring workers' general safety. These major actors must collaboratively engage in dialogue and an exchange of ideas to improve working conditions and boost workforce productivity.

On-the job training is a vital, and often overlooked resource for success that employers need to enact to improve productivity. Additionally, Kenyan employers must make a conscious effort to frequently liaise with training institutions on skills that are in market demand. Although this is critical, EAI's entry-level skills survey reveals that only 2 per cent and 10 per cent of informal and formal sector employers, respectively, reported any collaboration with TVET (technical and vocational education and training) or other training institutions on training students, curriculum development or internship placement. In addition, employers cited barriers to on the job training such as prohibitive costs, fear of trained staff being poached by competitors, and a lack of internal capacity to train.

On the other hand, trade unions need to encourage cooperative relations between employees and employers. Unions are responsible for setting up committees to provide training, education and resources for the advancement of workers. As a result, the industry will benefit from adequately skilled employees, reduced skill gaps and increased employment rates throughout the country. Trade unions also need to leverage their partnerships and networks with government and the private sector to link workforce with industry.
Finally, the government has the central duty of creating an enabling environment for investors and employers to ensure reasonable pay for all employees so workers earn a livable wage.

As we commemorate Labour Day this year, Kenyan workers should keep in mind the government's recent COVID-19 driven measures to reduce taxes (like VAT and PAYE), consequently providing a temporary cushion from financial burdens.

Overall, the government, labour unions, employers and academia must engage in a serious dialogue on creating a sustainable plan to prioritise worker's rights. Most importantly, workers should not have to wait for Labour Day to be granted mere wage increments, but rather should be paid a living wage from the start.
Lucy Mbuvi is a Research Associate at the Aga Khan University's East Africa Institute.
